Summary

This paper studies test-time adaptation for concept bottleneck models built on top of foundation models, under distribution shift. The authors argue that concept-based pipelines are not automatically robust after deployment, and propose CONDA, a three-stage adaptation method consisting of concept-score alignment, linear probing adaptation, and a residual concept bottleneck. The method uses only unlabeled target data and no source dataset access. The paper evaluates on CIFAR10-C, CIFAR100-C, Waterbirds, Metashift, and Camelyon17, and reports substantial gains over unadapted concept bottlenecks, sometimes approaching or exceeding non-interpretable baselines. The paper also includes interpretability analyses and runtime measurements.

Overall assessment

The paper addresses an important and timely problem: how to preserve interpretability while adapting foundation-model-based concept bottlenecks under test-time distribution shift. The motivation is strong, the empirical scope is broad, and the paper is clearly written at a high level. I also appreciate that the authors explicitly separate different failure modes and design different adaptation components for each. That said, I have several concerns about the methodological novelty, the strength of the theoretical framing, and the reliability of some empirical claims. In particular, the adaptation procedure appears to rely heavily on pseudo-label quality and on access to source-domain concept statistics, which somewhat weakens the “source-free” framing. The paper would benefit from a more careful comparison to existing test-time adaptation methods and a more rigorous analysis of when and why the proposed objectives work.

Strengths

1. Important problem setting.
The intersection of interpretability, foundation models, and test-time adaptation is highly relevant. The paper correctly identifies that concept bottlenecks can degrade under shift and that interpretability alone does not guarantee robustness.

2. Clear decomposition of failure modes.
The taxonomy into low-level shift, concept-level shift, and incomplete concept set is useful as a conceptual lens. Even if the formalization is somewhat idealized, it helps organize the design of the method.

3. Practical adaptation framework.
CONDA is modular and easy to understand: align concepts, adapt the classifier, then add residual concepts if needed. This staged design is intuitive and likely useful in practice.

4. Broad empirical evaluation.
The paper evaluates across multiple datasets, backbone models, and concept-bottleneck construction methods. This breadth is a real strength, and the runtime table is also helpful.

5. Interpretability analysis.
The residual concept analysis and the before/after explanation examples are valuable. It is good to see the authors not only report accuracy but also inspect how concept-to-class mappings change after adaptation.

Weaknesses and concerns

1. The “source-free” claim is somewhat overstated.
Although the source dataset is not used during adaptation, the method still assumes access to source-domain concept-score statistics, specifically class-conditional means and covariances. For many real deployments, these statistics may not be readily available, especially if the source data are inaccessible. This is an important assumption and should be emphasized more prominently as part of the method’s requirements.

2. Heavy dependence on pseudo-label quality.
The method’s success appears to depend strongly on pseudo-labels from zero-shot and linear-probing predictors. The paper acknowledges this limitation, but it is central rather than incidental. In settings where the foundation model is weak or miscalibrated, the adaptation can hurt performance. This makes the method less robust than the main narrative suggests.

3. The theoretical framing is not fully convincing.
The definitions of low-level shift and concept-level shift are intuitive, but the formalization is somewhat restrictive and not clearly connected to realistic distribution shift scenarios. In particular, the notion that prediction distributions remain identical under concept-level shift while concept distributions change seems more like a desideratum than a property that can be assumed in practice. The “completeness” definition is also quite strong and not operationalized.

4. Novelty relative to existing TTA and CBM work is moderate.
The method combines known ingredients: class-aware alignment, pseudo-labeling, elastic-net regularization, and residual branches. The combination is sensible, but the paper should be more careful in distinguishing its contribution from prior test-time adaptation methods and from recent residual concept bottleneck work. The residual branch in particular feels close in spirit to existing residual or incremental CBM ideas.

5. Some empirical comparisons are incomplete.
The paper compares against zero-shot, linear probing, and several CBM variants, but it is less clear how CONDA compares to strong generic test-time adaptation baselines applied directly to the foundation-model classifier or to the concept predictor. Since the paper’s claim is about deployment under shift, such comparisons are important.

6. Interpretability claims need more caution.
The residual concepts are annotated automatically, but automatic annotation is noisy and may not faithfully reflect human interpretability. The paper presents these annotations as evidence of improved interpretability, but the evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive. Also, adding residual concepts increases model complexity, which may reduce interpretability even if the concepts are semantically meaningful.

7. Some results appear dataset- and backbone-dependent.
The gains are strong in several settings, but not uniformly so. In some cases, adaptation does not help or can even hurt. The paper does acknowledge this in the limitations, but the main text could better reflect the conditional nature of the gains.

Questions for the authors

1. How much of CONDA’s gain comes from the residual branch versus the concept-score alignment and classifier adaptation? The ablation suggests different components matter in different shifts, but can the authors quantify the marginal contribution more systematically across all datasets?

2. What happens if the source-domain class-conditional concept statistics are estimated noisily or are unavailable? Can the method be adapted to a fully source-free setting?

3. How sensitive is CONDA to pseudo-label calibration? Would temperature scaling or confidence filtering materially improve stability?

4. Can the authors compare against generic TTA methods applied directly to the backbone or linear probe, to better isolate the benefit of concept-based adaptation?

5. How stable are the learned residual concepts across random seeds and batches? Are the same semantic concepts recovered consistently?

6. The concept-level shift definition assumes prediction distributions can remain unchanged while concept distributions shift. Can the authors provide a more operational characterization or empirical test for this regime?

Suggestions for improvement

1. Clarify assumptions.
Explicitly list all information required at adaptation time, including source concept statistics, and discuss deployment scenarios where these are realistic.

2. Strengthen baselines.
Add stronger comparisons to standard TTA methods and perhaps to residual adaptation methods not specific to CBMs.

3. Improve theoretical discussion.
Either weaken the formal claims or provide more rigorous justification for the proposed objectives and shift taxonomy.

4. Report calibration and pseudo-label quality.
Since pseudo-labeling is central, it would be useful to report pseudo-label accuracy or confidence statistics where possible.

5. Discuss interpretability more carefully.
Separate semantic plausibility of residual concepts from true human interpretability, and acknowledge the tradeoff between added flexibility and simplicity.

6. Provide failure case analysis.
The negative results in the appendix are important. A more prominent discussion of when CONDA fails would improve the paper’s credibility.

Overall recommendation

I find the paper promising and relevant, with a solid empirical story and a useful practical framework. However, I do not think the current version fully justifies some of its broader claims, especially around source-free adaptation and interpretability under shift. The method is interesting, but the assumptions and limitations should be more clearly stated, and the empirical comparison should be strengthened.

Score: 6/10

Confidence: 4/5

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper proposes CONDA, a test-time adaptation framework for concept bottleneck models built on foundation models under distribution shift. It identifies three failure modes—non-robust concepts under low-level shift, non-robust classifiers under concept-level shift, and incomplete concept sets—and addresses them with a three-stage adaptation procedure: concept-score alignment, linear probing adaptation, and a residual concept bottleneck. Experiments on CIFAR-C, Waterbirds, Metashift, and Camelyon17 suggest substantial gains over unadapted CBMs and, in some cases, parity with or improvement over non-interpretable baselines.
strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: combining interpretability, foundation models, and test-time adaptation under distribution shift.
Clear decomposition of failure modes and a corresponding modular adaptation strategy, which makes the method conceptually easy to follow.
Broad empirical evaluation across multiple datasets, shift types, and CBM construction methods.
The paper reports both average and worst-group accuracy, which is appropriate for robustness analysis.
Interpretability analysis is a useful addition, especially the residual concept bottleneck and concept annotation examples.
The method is practical in the sense that it uses unlabeled target data only and does not require access to source training data during adaptation.
weaknesses: The method relies heavily on pseudo-label quality, which can be brittle and may undermine the claimed robustness gains.

Several components appear heuristic rather than principled, including the Gaussian modeling for concept alignment, the batchwise online adaptation scheme, and the choice of regularizers/hyperparameters.
The theoretical framing of distribution shifts and concept completeness is somewhat informal and does not yield strong guarantees.
The residual concept bottleneck improves accuracy, but it may also complicate interpretability; the paper acknowledges this tradeoff only partially.
Some reported gains depend on strong backbone models and favorable pseudo-labeling, raising questions about how general the approach is across weaker or less aligned foundation models.
The paper’s claims of being the first to address this setting are difficult to verify and may overstate novelty relative to adjacent test-time adaptation and concept-based explanation work.
soundness_issues: The assumption that source-domain class-conditional concept-score distributions are Gaussian is strong and not justified empirically; if violated, the CSA objective may be poorly matched to the data.

The Mahalanobis-based alignment objective depends on source statistics that are assumed available even though the source dataset is unavailable; this is plausible but should be more explicitly justified as a deployment assumption.

Pseudo-labels are generated from zero-shot and linear-probing predictors, but the adaptation procedure then optimizes against these potentially noisy labels; this creates a circular dependency that can cause confirmation bias.

The definition of low-level shift as preserving concept-score distributions and concept-level shift as preserving prediction distributions is somewhat idealized and may not correspond cleanly to real-world shifts.
The completeness definition is not operationalized in a way that can be tested or estimated, so the failure-mode taxonomy is more descriptive than actionable.

The residual branch is added to the main CBM, but the paper does not fully analyze whether this preserves the intended interpretability of the bottleneck or simply turns the model into a larger linear classifier with concept-like features.
Some complexity and runtime claims appear optimistic given the dependence on foundation-model inference and repeated batchwise adaptation; the practical cost may be higher in real deployments.
The empirical comparisons mix different CBM construction methods and backbones, which is useful, but the fairness of comparisons is not always fully transparent from the description alone.
